summary: Current location configuration protocols can give a host a location URI, but they lack a way for the host to inspect or set the privacy rules applied to those URIs. This document extends them to let hosts do so.

plainLanguage.summary: Your address might be shared. This lets you see and set who may look at it.

questions: how to set location privacy policy in held
what is the empty policy in location configuration
subtitle: How a host can see and change the privacy rules attached to its location URI, using a second URI.

tldr.problem: A location server can hand a host a location URI, but the host has no way to see or change the privacy rules the server applies when others use that URI.
tldr.mechanism: The server also hands out a policy URI, an HTTP or HTTPS address the host can GET, PUT and DELETE to read, replace or remove the authorization policy. HELD gets two small extension elements to carry it.
tldr.outcome: Hosts can restrict who sees their location before sharing the location URI. The policy URI is a shared secret, so it must be unguessable and protected like a password.

today: RFC 7199 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2014. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Hosts that use location-based services first need to learn their own location. A Location Configuration Protocol (LCP) lets a location provider, such as a local access network, tell a host where it is. This can be done by value (coordinates or a civic address) or by reference (a URI that others can dereference to get the location).

Location by reference has a privacy benefit: the dereference step is a point where policy can be enforced. But existing LCPs give the host no way to tell the Location Server how its location should be handled. RFC 7199 closes that gap. It defines policy URIs and extends the HELD protocol to carry them, so a host acting as the Rule Maker can inspect and modify the policy for its own location URIs.
sections.plainLanguage: Your host gets a link that others can use to find out where it is. This document gives the host a second link to control who is allowed to use the first.

sections.title: Policy URIs
sections.content:
A policy URI is an HTTP or HTTPS URI that identifies a policy resource holding the authorization policy for a linked location resource. A Rule Maker uses it to inspect and install policy documents that tell the Location Server how to protect that location. The resource can always be represented as a common-policy document (RFC 4745), possibly with extensions such as geolocation policy (RFC 6772).

The Location Server creates the policy URI at the same moment as the location URI it controls, and the two MUST be different. Each location URI has either one policy URI or none. The initial policy behind a policy URI MUST match the policy that would apply if there were no policy URI, so a client that ignores policy URIs keeps working as before.

A policy URI is only valid while its location URI set is valid. Once the set expires, the server MUST NOT respond to requests to the policy URI.
sections.plainLanguage: The second link is made at the same time as the first and works only as long as the first one does. If you never use it, everything works as it did before.

sections.title: Reading, Replacing and Deleting Policy
sections.content:
A Location Server that is the authority for policy URIs MUST support three HTTP methods on them:

  • GET returns the complete current policy in a 200 response.
  • PUT replaces the policy with a complete document in the request body. The server MUST validate it first.
  • DELETE removes the policy. The server MUST then refuse access to the location URIs it governs until a new policy is put in place.

The server MUST support the common-policy format, media type application/auth-policy+xml, and it is the default for GET requests without an Accept header. Knowing the policy URI counts as enough proof of authorization, though a server MAY deny requests by local policy, for example by allowing GET but not PUT, or by requiring HTTP or TLS client authentication.

A location URI can become invalid in three ways: a validity interval in the policy ends, the policy is deleted, or the validity interval set by the LCP expires. The first two are temporary because the policy URI can be used to fix them. The last is permanent.
sections.plainLanguage: With the secret link you can look at the rules, swap them for new ones, or throw them away. If you throw them away, nobody can see your location until you write new rules.

sections.title: Policy Defaults
sections.content:
Setting no policy is very different from setting an empty policy. The empty policy is a ruleset with no rules. Because the policy language is default-deny, it tells the server never to give out the location. If a client never touches the policy URI, it tacitly accepts whatever the server applies, which can mean location for anyone who has the location URI.

For HELD, a client should assume the default policy grants any requester access as long as they hold the location URI. To make it less permissive, the client updates the policy before it distributes the location URI.

Servers face a similar choice. A server does not know whether a client understands policy URIs, so its default has to be open enough to be useful. Once a client includes requestPolicyUri in its request, the server may switch to something more restrictive, even the empty policy, because the client can loosen it if it wants. Implementers should decide deliberately what to do when a user gives no privacy input.
sections.plainLanguage: No rules at all and an empty list of rules are different. No rules means the server does what it likes. An empty list means nobody gets in.

sections.title: The HELD Extension
sections.content:
HELD (RFC 5985) returns a locationUriSet, a set of location URIs that share one access control policy. RFC 7199 adds two elements in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:geopriv:held:policy:

  • requestPolicyUri, an empty element a client adds to a location request to say it wants a policy URI.
  • policyUri, a URI element in the location response that carries the policy URI.

The URI in policyUri MUST be a policy URI as described above and MUST use the http: or https: scheme. A server decides by local policy whether to provide one even without a request.

Because later documents might allow other protocols, clients MUST check the scheme of any policy URI received from HELD. If it is not http: or https:, the client MUST discard it and behave as if none was provided.
sections.plainLanguage: The client can add a note saying it wants a secret control link. The server then adds that link to its answer. If the link looks strange, the client ignores it.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC walks through one exchange. A client asks for a location URI and a policy URI. The response contains a locationUriSet with two location URIs (one https:, one sip:) and a policyUri. The client then does a GET and sees a default policy that provides location to any requester who knows the location URI.

Disliking that, the client sends a PUT with a new policy: only one friend, identified as sip:friend@example.com, may get location, and only at city level. The server replies 200. Later, to invalidate the URI permanently, the client sends a DELETE and gets 200.
sections.plainLanguage: You look at the default rules, replace them with rules that let only one friend see your city, and later cancel the link altogether.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Two risks matter: someone manipulating policy to grant or deny access wrongly, and disclosure of the policy itself. So both the policy URI and the policy document must travel with integrity and confidentiality. The server SHOULD give out https: policy URIs and require TLS. An http: URI MAY be used if other protection exists, but servers SHOULD reject PUT and DELETE on http: policy URIs. When neither application-layer nor network-layer security is present, servers MUST reject PUT and DELETE.

Since possession of the URI is the only credential, the server MUST make it impractical to guess, even for an attacker who has requested many policy URIs. It MUST NOT derive the URI only from public information such as the target identity or a location URI, and adding 128 bits or more of random entropy is RECOMMENDED. Servers SHOULD rate limit clients to (2^(N/2))/T queries per second, where N is the bits of entropy and T the lifetime in seconds. With N=128 the probability of compromise is at most 5.4e-20 under this scheme.

Each target MUST get a different location URI and policy URI. Otherwise an outsider could tell that targets sharing a URI are in the same place, and targets could see and change each other's policy. A server MUST create new URIs for every request unless requests can be reliably identified as coming from the same client, for example behind a middlebox. Clients SHOULD treat policy URIs like passwords and not send them to other hosts or store them in plaintext.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret link works like a password, so it has to be hard to guess, sent privately and never shared. Every person gets their own link.
